title: Flora's Wobbly Play
markdown:
Flora the rabbit was prone to flutters. Nico the mole was wonderfully steady. They lived in a cozy hollow under an old oak on the edge of Whispering Woods, and they were putting on a play: The Tale of the Grumpy Cloud.

Flora was enthusiastic and, when it came to forest audiences, a professional worrier. Ears twitched. Forgotten lines. Misplaced props. A rain shower on the day. Her beady eyes darted, looking for trouble that had not arrived.

Nico was as steady as a moss-covered stone in a sunny spot. When he rumpled his velvet fur it was usually from a contented sigh after a juicy grub, not from fuss. An earthy smell lived around him. Paws ready. Voice like warm earth after spring rain.

“The stage is set,” he said, soft. “Toadstool seats. Leaves rustling for sound. Quite perfect.”

Flora was not listening. She sat on a plump mossy log, nose in a very large, very old book that smelled of dried leaves: Flora’s Big Book of Playtime Worries, looping letters, so big it was a wonder she could carry it.

“What if I forget the sunbeam line? What if a squirrel steals the pretend moon from its string? What if a badger auditions mid-play?” Tail flick.

Nico’s pebble-eyes blinked. “No badgers invited. We have practised the sunbeam lines fifty times. You know them in your sleep.”

“But the book!” She patted it. “Backup plans. Forgotten lines: Plan A, a helpful echo from the trees. Plan B, a dramatic sniffle and a loud stage whisper. Plan C—” conspiratorial “—the entire cast improvises a cheerful song about lost thoughts and where they scurried.”

From a high branch Miss Amber, their owl teacher, spoke softly. Spectacles sat comically on her beak. Flowers nodded. Sunbeams brightened. “A thorough book. Impressive preparedness. Sometimes the best performances have a sprinkle of the unexpected.”

Play day: the clearing bustled. Friends from all corners of Whispering Woods. Butterflies on the audience edge, silk wings nervous. Ladybugs on the nearest leaves taking notes in tiny berry-ink notebooks, as if the play might be examined later. The toadstool seats filled. The leaves rustled on cue, and also when they felt like it.

Flora, dressed as a worried bright Sunbeam, felt a wobble in her whiskers. “Oh. What shall I do?”

Nico, a large wonderfully grumpy cloud of dandelion fluff, nodded. “Normal, before something important. What’s the contingency?”

From an acorn pouch she produced a smooth shiny pebble. “Backup for wobbly whiskers: hold a lucky pebble.” Grip. Breath. Wobble lessened.

Nico began his most important line — “I don’t want to shine today, it’s far too much effort” — when a tiny over-enthusiastic ladybug, helpful, scurried onstage to polish the cloud. “A stage-invading insect! Unforeseen audience participation! Plan G: the polite leaf brush!” From behind a fern, a big soft dewy maple leaf. She ushered the ladybug away, gentle and firm. Nico, taken aback, added an extra grumble. The audience chuckled.

Then a real playful gust rustled the leaves and sent the pretend moon — a wobbly paper lantern — off its string into the bushes, dandelion fluff in its wake. “Emergency! Celestial displacement! Plan K: the moon-rescue rhyme!” She launched a hurried chant about a moon on a brief adventure that needed a nudge home.

Nico’s smile grew. The more peculiar the backups, the sillier and better the play. When she was meant to speak of a rainbow after the cloud cried, she used Plan M: juggling three perfectly round acorns, because, she explained with great seriousness, “the colours of the sky are happy little balls that sometimes like to dance.” They bounced delightfully.

Miss Amber’s chuckles were warm. The audience, first confused, began to giggle. They loved each peculiar item. The ladybug enjoyed the leaf. The acorns had happy energy.

Nico had the time of his life. He had never played a grumpier cloud, or a funnier one. Extra grumbles, puffing, shielding his eyes from imaginary sun, just to see what she would produce next. The grumpy cloud had become an adventure.

A flourish of dandelion puff, a grand bow, the Compendium still open. Applause, chirps, buzzes.

Flora’s whiskers quivered with exhaustion and pride. “Was it all right? It wasn’t quite like we practised.”

Nico rumpled, immense happiness. “The best play I’ve been in. We didn’t follow the script. The audience loved it.”

Miss Amber landed on a low bough, spectacles adjusted. “The book is full of clever plans. Good to be prepared. The moments that make us laugh are often the ones that are not written down. You two made something new. Splendid.”

Flora looked at smiling faces, ladybugs beaming, butterflies applauding with wings. The Compendium felt less like a shield and more like a collection of memories. Wobbly whiskers, polite leaf, juggling acorns — unexpected, and from the heart.

She logged pebble-grip / leaf-brush / moon rhyme / dancing acorns in the back of the Worries book, under a new heading she invented: things that worked because they were not in the book. She left the paper lantern in the bushes as a souvenir the wind could visit, and let Nico keep one extra grumble for next year’s cloud. The ladybug sat on a programme and looked polished. The clearing, toadstools still arranged, had hosted a play that planned itself halfway through and was better for it.
